name: Archet Hunting Bow
entries: Purchasing a famed Archet hunting bow is not a matter of simply paying the right price. Player-heroes wishing to acquire a bow will need to both prove themselves worthy and perform some great deed of service to the people of Archet. For example, a Player-hero may address some danger in the {@book Chetwood|TLotRR|8|The Chetwood} or the {@book Weather Hills|TLotRR|8|The Weather Hills}, protecting a group of woodsmen who have encountered some trouble while felling trees in the forest, or anything else the Loremaster deems appropriate to their campaign.

Once a Player-hero has proven worthy, they must then demonstrate that they are a skilled archer by spending three days on a solitary hunt in the Chetwood, and returning with a buck of no less than ten points (a {@dc 20} Wisdom ({@skill Hunting|TLotRR}) check; the Player-hero can make two rolls each day, and has three days to complete the task).
After completing this, the Player-hero can choose the Archet hunting bow as their next reward, or replace one of their rewards with it.

entries: "Once you unlock the secrets of brewin' Bloodsbane, set up shop in Dis and Styx. The servants of Dispater and Moloch can't get enough of it, especially the floral stuff. And I know a knight or a mage or two in Sutekh and Asmodeus's service who'll pay no small sum for a bottle or two with nightshade.
But if you share the means to make it with anyone, the last thing you'll smell will be parchment, sulfur, and something sweet."

entries.name: The Four Sacred Artifacts
entries: Four Sacred Artifacts appeared at the dawn of the Bürach Empire, each a divine gift from the four gods: Aurelia, Galt, Maligant, and Ulmyr. These relics were given to Bürach's first emperor, Indorius I, and inherited by each of his successors.

Maligant provided the mighty sword, Dämglesvir, to slay Bürach's enemies. Galt placed a crown on Indorius I's head to signify his divine right. Ulmyr gifted the emperor an orb of foresight to make him a wise ruler. Aurelia clad him in a breastplate, wishing only to protect him and his heirs.

Many centuries later, after Emperor Leopold I was assassinated, custody of the artifacts sparked a civil war. Each of the holy treasures disappeared amid the fighting. One religiously fervent tale claims they blazed with radiant light before banishing themselves beyond mortal reach. Other rumors suggest they were each stolen or lost in various separate conspiracies. It's certain that whoever holds the Sacred Artifacts controls the fate of the Bürach Empire.

entries.name: Wielding An Artifact
entries: Before disappearing, the artifacts were tarnished and corrupted by Emperor Leopold I's delusions, cruelty, and malice. Darkness had seeped into them, transforming their divine power and purpose. Though it's heretical to suggest, some believe the artifacts' befoulment is somehow linked to the death of the gods and the growing influence of the Great Beast.

Wielding even one Sacred Artifact is difficult. Their true power can only be unlocked by practicing their use. Yet this necessitates more time exposed to the darkness that now infuses them, which can infest the wielder's body and mind.

entries.name: Attunement and Proficiency
entries: Each Sacred Artifact has three tiers of {@variantrule Attunement|XPHB} available to its user. When a character attunes to the item, they have access only to the benefits (and the curse) listed under the Aspirant tier. The Adept and Master tiers of {@variantrule Attunement|XPHB} are unlocked over time (see Attunement Milestones, below).
{@variantrule Attunement|XPHB} to a Sacred Artifact can't be voluntarily ended. If the {@variantrule Attunement|XPHB} does end, the character can attune to the item again at the Aspirant tier.

Each artifact also curses its wielder. In addition to the curse effects listed for each tier, a character attuned to a Sacred Artifact is unwilling to part with the item, keeping it within reach at all times. If the artifact's curse is ended or suppressed, the character's {@variantrule Attunement|XPHB} with that item is broken.

entries.name: Attunement Milestones
entries: To ascend to a higher tier of {@variantrule Attunement|XPHB} and unlock additional powers of a Sacred Artifact, the attuned character must achieve a specific milestone. There is no minimum level required to achieve a milestone. However, Adept-tier artifacts are appropriate for characters of level 5 to 10, while Master-tier artifacts are appropriate for characters of level 11 and above.
The GM and players should work together to create appropriate milestones for the campaign, using these examples (themed to the four artifacts) as guidance:

items: Wield {@i {@item Dämglesvir|GrimHollowCG24}} to slay a mighty foe.
Take no damage during a difficult combat.
Earn the fealty of an important ruler.
You alter a future witnessed in {@i {@item Ulmyr's Eye|GrimHollowCG24}}.

entries.name: Shared Delusions
entries: The darkness that seeped into the Sacred Artifacts causes their wielders to experience the same paranoid delusions that plagued Emperor Leopold I.

All characters attuned to a Sacred Artifact suffer the same delusions, which could include the sense of being watched, believing a {@variantrule Friendly [Attitude]|XPHB|Friendly} NPC to be {@variantrule Hostile [Attitude]|XPHB|Hostile} , or mistaking an innocent person or household pet for a monster. Characters can even experience multiple simultaneous delusions.

A character suffering a delusion can use the {@action Search|XPHB} action to discern the truth, typically by succeeding on a {@dc 20} (or higher) Wisdom ({@skill Insight|XPHB} or {@skill Perception|XPHB}) check.

If the GM is using the {@variantrule Influence Dice|GrimHollowCG24|Influence Dice rules} rules, the frequency and intensity of delusions increases while the number of dice in the Beast Pool exceeds the number of dice in the Resolve Pool.

entries.name: Might of Heaven
entries: Dämglesvir was one of the many weapons wielded by Maligant himself during the Aetheric War. One of the god's most powerful armaments, its name means {@i "might of heaven."}

Dämglesvir was brought to Emperor Indorius I by a celestial honor guard. The weapon's siblings are wielded by Maligant's former lieutenants: the Arch Seraph Empyreus wields Judgement, while the Arch Daemon Tormach brandishes Wrath.

images.altText: Black leather armor with intricate embroidery, the shoulders consisting of black raven feathers.

entries.name: Dragonmark Focus Item
entries: Much of the influence of the dragonmarked houses is based on a simple principle: it's easier to amplify an existing magical effect, such as that of a dragonmark, than to create the same effect from nothing. Taken on their own, the powers granted by dragonmarks aren't overwhelmingly powerful. However, over the course of centuries, House Cannith and the Twelve have developed items that focus and enhance the powers of the mark to produce powerful, reliable effects. In many cases—such as the Storm Spires of House Lyrandar and the Creation Forges of House Cannith—the Arcane Congress has been unable to duplicate the effects of these powerful focus items for non-dragonmarked creatures. Other items have since been reproduced in forms that anyone can use, but an item that requires the user to possess a specific dragonmark is always easier to create and less expensive than one that produces the same effect for anyone, giving the dragonmarked houses an important advantage.

In addition, you could have a dragonmark focus item that produces the same effect as an existing magic item from the Dungeon Master's Guide—except it can't be used or attuned unless you possess a particular dragonmark. House Lyrandar is working on a version of a {@item Broom of Flying|XDMG} for dragonmarked heirs, though they haven't perfected it yet. House Ghallanda is developing a {@i Portable Inn}—a version of the {@item Daern's Instant Fortress||Instant Fortress}—but it's proven difficult. It's always up to the DM to decide if there's a dragonmark focus item that replicates the effects of any given magic item, and if so, how readily it's available.

The Dragonmark Focus Items table provides examples of focus items, along with the item whose effects they reproduce and the mark required to use or attune to the focus item. A focus item's rarity is generally less than a similar item that anyone can use, reflecting the relative ease of manufacture. However, this doesn't mean they are readily available; dragonmark focus items are rarely sold in stores. They can only be created using proprietary tools, and are produced exclusively by House Cannith and the Twelve for use by trusted agents of the dragonmarked houses. So while many Medani inquisitives wear {@item Medi Spectacles|ExploringEberron24}, they acquired them through service to the house, not by purchasing them with gold.

While a dragonmark focus item usually has the same general appearance as the item whose effects it duplicates, it bears the image of the required mark somewhere on the item, and often carries the sigil of the associated house. Siberys dragonshards are a vital component of focus items, most including a shard in some form. With that said, a focus item's design can differ from the usual magic item's form—the {@item Serpentine Mirror|ExploringEberron24} has a similar effect to a {@item Crystal Ball|XDMG}, but it's a flat mirror as opposed to an orb.

entries.name: House Products
entries: The dragonmarked houses form the foundation of Khorvaire's magical economy, and they're the source of many of the magic items you can buy in the Five Nations. 90% of {@item Potions of Healing|XDMG} are either made by House Jorasco or produced according to their specifications. If you have two +1 Shortswords produced by a Cannith forge, they'll be essentially identical, while an Aereni {@item Shortsword|XPHB} would be lovingly crafted by a particular artisan.

In dealing with house products, consider whether the item is military or civilian in nature. During the war, a large portion of House Cannith's manufactured goods were designed for military use. If you buy a {@item Cloak of Protection|XDMG} from a Cannith dealer in Sharn, is it an elegant model made for a noble to wear to the Tain Gala, or is it a Brelish Bear cloak, originally issued to an elite commando? If an item is essentially a tool of war, then it may have actually been used in the war; if so, which nation was it made for? Is it legitimate surplus? Was it likely sold by a retired soldier, or salvaged from a battlefield?

Military gear is often more functional than decorative. It may bear the markings of a particular nation, and it's possible it shows signs of use. On the other hand, civilian products need to lure in customers. Consider a {@item Potion of Healing|XDMG}. The potions Jorasco sold to the Brelish army were known as "coppers" because of the coppery taste of the fluid, and the potency is clearly marked for accurate administration; a Brelish soldier might call a {@item Potion of Superior Healing|XDMG} a "copper-3." By contrast, a civilian {@item Potion of Healing|XDMG} could be called something like "Vivacity," with a shiny label and available in a variety of flavors. You might find a barker in a part of town where the people are wealthy enough to buy such a product. "Feeling worn down? Perhaps you've had a little fall? Get back on your feet with a shot of Vivacity!"

images.altText: A longbow made of wood and dark green vines wrapping around it, with intricate elvish designs.

entries: He was given to me by your father, little one. He kept us warm while your father and I trekked through the Dreemoth Ravine and the ruins of Draconia twenty years ago. Such vicious blizzards, the likes of which are only topped by the Neverfields—or Eiselcross, so I've heard. You should have seen us, marching through the snow, dozens of Ashari cloaked in flame, melting trenches in the rime as they advanced, and me, my furs pulled around my nose, blinking through the snow, holding tight to this little one.

When your father returned to Pyrah, I feared I'd never see our little flamefriend again, but.... Here, hold him, hear his little elemental heart fluttering. Think of your father when you feel that warmth, protecting you, watching over you. No matter where in the world you are, whether you're near Pyrah or far, he'll be a bit of family, and a bit of home.
entries.from: to his goddaughter, Ev of Pyrah

name: Galvanized Claw
entries: Ripping the flesh of the beasts they slay to fashion ferocious weapons is something hunters have gotten remarkably good at over the course of their hunts.

entries.name: Goddess's Protection
entries: After the Aetheric War, Aurelia was desperate to protect what remained of mortal life. Yet the goddess was heartsick from the slaughter and did not wish to create another weapon. Instead, she ensured that no danger to the emperor's life could ever threaten the stability of the realm.
The Hearthfire Breastplate sheathed the emperor in golden light, making their presence a beacon of hope and safety in the Bürach Empire.

name: Heliana's Guide to Monster Hunting (very rare)

entries.name: Rules Tip: Pushing and Shoving
entries: Certain character options, such as the Path of the Juggernaut barbarian in {@book chapter 4|TalDoreiCampaignSettingReborn|3}, grant the ability to push other creatures around the battlefield with your attacks. But this is just one way to push a creature. If you want to move a creature without hurting it, there's a {@action shove|PHB|special shove attack} available to all characters. The {@book Vestige of Divergence|TalDoreiCampaignSettingReborn|5|Vestiges of Divergence} Honor's Last Stand encourages you to shove your foes away while you valiantly stand your ground.

entries.name: Divine Authority
entries: Galt imagined the Bürach Empire as a glorious society of fairness and order. To ensure that it operated effectively, it would need a unifying voice that spoke with divine authority.
Indorius's Crown is named for the emperor who wore it first, and each of Indorius's heirs have felt the weight of authority upon their own head.

images.altText: An intricate silver necklace with emerald gems.

images.title: Left: Short Spear, Great Spear, Mattock; Right: Bow, Great Bow

images.altText: Mirror of Infinite Transpondence: a silver, handheld mirror with intricate designs all around. A face is carved at the top of the handle, and an eye at the top of the mirror. Inside the mirror is a picture of a stone tower with a wind-torn cloth peak.

entries: Though the name of the champion who wielded Mythcarver has been lost, legend says that the songs she sung in her beautiful contralto made her friends rejoice and her enemies weep with fear. Mythcarver was forged in the flying city of Zemniaz by a master arcanist and blacksmith along with the wielder herself, who wove song and spell into the blade with each fold of the metal.

images.altText: An elegant rapier with a swept hilt.

Golden plate mail with black fabric wrapped around the waist. Throughout the armor are intricate designs. In center and upon the left shoulder pauldron is the symbol of the Dawnfather - a solitary sun with eight rays.
A maul embedded with an orange gemstone emitting flames from the head of the weapon.

name: Revelations
entries: Made of an unknown metal that mixes blood and steel, this ghastly sword is studded with dozens of eyes from various creatures that stare hungrily at all who are confronted with it. Only a competent hunter can wield a weapon of such weight, but armed with it, they will never lose sight of their prey and will never be caught in an ambush. Such a dangerous weapon should only be used with the utmost caution.

entries.name: Jarlpact Rings
entries: Long ago, a set of rings was crafted to help cement a truce between warring tribes of giants. Four rival giant jarls met to don their rings in a show of peace. However, the truce lasted only until the celebratory feast, when the drunken jarls started a brawl that became a bloody combat. The rings shattered along with the peace, but fragments of the original artifacts shaped themselves into smaller versions of the rings and scattered across the Northlands.

In addition to their base powers, each ring grants an additional jarlpact benefit if at least one other jarlpact ring is attuned to a nearby ally. This benefit doesn't apply to multiple rings worn by the same character.

name: Shard of Moonlight
entries: This weapon is the flesh of a Great One carved away in pain and fashioned into a blade. The Shard of Moonlight is the reason the Shattered Moon exists and the Devouring Moon is no more. He who wields the blade is overwhelmed by hope, however misguided it might be...

name: Shroud of Ending
entries: There is an old tale about a foolish birdfolk sage who believed themselves to be even wiser than the Amaranthine. One day, while wandering alone in the Wood at night, they met Tyton, who had come to collect their soul. Rather than accept their death with dignity, the sage instead debated with {@deity Tyton|Amaranthine|HumblewoodCampaignSetting} about the unfairness of mortality. {@deity Tyton|Amaranthine|HumblewoodCampaignSetting} could not deny their logic, but warned the heedless sage about disrupting the cycle of life and death. He wove a cloak from the fabric of the night sky itself, infused it with a small fraction of his power, and gifted it to the sage. With this, the sage could live forever. {@deity Tyton|Amaranthine|HumblewoodCampaignSetting} declared that he would return in a century, and if the sage still felt the same, the Amaranthine of death would never again visit them. For a hundred years, the sage watched everyone around them gradually age, succumbing to illness and death as they lived on. In the end, the sage understood their folly and asked for {@deity Tyton|Amaranthine|HumblewoodCampaignSetting} to guide them peacefully into the hereafter. It is said that {@deity Tyton|Amaranthine|HumblewoodCampaignSetting} left the Shroud of Ending in the world as a reminder of the sage's foolishness.

name: Skinchanger Arm Ring
entries: This arm ring is made from copper and is covered with a patina that cannot be removed.

There was once a sect of Northern warriors dedicated to learning from the animals in their region. Each member of the order sought to exemplify the capabilities and spirit of their chosen animal. The raven warrior was keen to observe and could travel far and fast. The follower of the wolf fought well in conjunction with others. Others had strength and endurance like bears.

These ideals were forged into an enchanted arm ring worn by the leader of the sect. Whether this magic was achieved with the aid of dwarves, druids, or sorcerers, none can say. With experience, the wearer of the arm ring could shapeshift into one of the three animals exemplified by the warriors.

Though the order won many victories on the battlefield, they couldn't be held in the employ of any one jarl. The wilds called to them, and they visited the settled lands of the North less and less as the years went by, until they were never seen again.

Oh! Oh gods, are you seriously asking me to explain it? Geez, sure, I'll try, but you really gotta feel it, you know? The sensation of the wind whipping past you as you shoot up into the sky, then—whoa!—your stomach just drops out from you, and it's like you left your heart behind as you start to fall. It's like nothing's holding onto you, then—whoosh!—the wind catches you, and swings you back into the sky.

images.altText: An Ashari woman with long orange hair flies on her white-winged skysail through a rocky canyon. She wears green clothing.
A skyship, its white sails entirely unfurled, flies through a dusky, red sky. The ship emanates a glowing, blue arcane magic below it, keeping it aloft.

entries: Records kept by the Birthheart temple in Vasselheim say that the Spire of Conflux was created when the Wildmother breathed on a young beech tree. The sapling transformed into a curving staff and the Wildmother's breath crystallized into the glowing jewel that hovers in its center. The bearer of this mythic staff can command the elements as if they were one with the enduring, yet ever-changing, landscape of Exandria itself...

images.altText: A twisted staff made of wood and vines shaped like a shepherd's crook with a glowing blue crystal in the center of the crook.

entries: Many weapons created by mortals during the Age of Arcanum were designed with hopes to surpass or even destroy the gods, but not so with Dwueth'var. That shining sword, bright with the light of the bold full moon and the enigmatic starlit night, was forged by acolytes of the Wildmother and the Moonweaver, united in their love of this fragile world and their determination to protect it.

images.altText: A silver greatsword with a red hilt. Inset in the hilt is a green gemstone. Runes run down the center of the blade, where also runs silver-white lines of magic.

name: Storrbani
entries: Thogar Giant-Hewer earned great renown through unwavering bravery but not intellectual brilliance. His unmatched courage often forged far ahead of his reason. As a youth, he could not prevent marauding giants and trolls from destroying his village and murdering his family. Left alone on the blood-soaked snow, a fire kindled deep in Thogar's heart. From that day, he unwaveringly sought vengeance against giantfolk, not for glory or renown but in the hope his daring might earn him friends or even a new family of his own.

The Giant-Hewer became a terror to trolls and giants alike. Though not the strongest warrior and certainly never the wisest, he braved troll dens and giant camps, throwing himself into battle where others paused to strategize. Yet time and again, the people he saved turned cold. His deeds, though brave, were rarely welcome. His plans resulted in the death of everyone but himself. His traps lured giants to their doom at the expense of entire villages. Those he rescued offered no feasts of thanks, only wary glances and closed doors. The more he gave, the more alone he became, yet still he fought on believing if he was only brave enough, he could win through to find a new family.

Thogar met his end in his own typical fashion. After running across the trail of a band of storm giants heading toward a village, he foolishly attacked them in the settlement square. His blade, Storrbani, slew many giants before the others fled, but unfortunately, the fires ignited by the battle burned down half the village. Thogar's shattered body lay in the remains of the wedding feast (to which the giants had been invited), and no one came to his aid or to witness his last breath. Skalds say he died utterly alone, but when the Valkyries came to collect him, he did not wish to enter Valhalla alone. Taking pity on the brave warrior, they cast his spirit into his blade, binding it there until the day he falls again, fighting beside a true friend, so together they might enter the Hall of Golden Shields side by side.

name: The Grave Blade
entries: The reavers of Wolfheim brought home many strange treasures as souvenirs and mementos from their campaigns abroad. A dwarven warrior named Essalla claimed a strange sword as her share of the spoils on one such raiding journey. Unusual in design and unadorned by dwarvish standards, it seemed destined to be a souvenir brought out only when tales of the campaign were to be told.
This sword has a dull, lifeless grey blade, and the hilt is carved from aged bone. The guard is made from ribs, and the pommel is sourced from the rounded end of a femur, both cast in bronze

The Grave Blade became known in different tales, for the threads of fate of each bearer seemed to be cut short soon after taking possession of it. It has changed hands many times over the next nine years, seemingly taken from a corpse as often as it was exchanged for gold or favors.

The blade is known for the song it hums in the presence of undead, and with the death of its carriers, the blade's song grows ever more insistent. Some say the song is a warning, while others theorize that it wants to be found and interred with the body of its first bearer.

The souvenir of so much death was lost among a merchant's wares that never reached their destination in Wolfheim, and the mystery of its song persists in tales told on dark nights when the fire burns low.

name: Tordalfr's Rebuttal
entries: Tordalfr was a storm giantkin born to a human mother in a small village. After years of jibes and taunts from the children of local warriors, he snapped.

Brael, son of the village headman, and a pompous, aspiring warrior, called Tordalfr out in public, proclaiming to his assembled cronies that there was irrefutable evidence that Tordalfr was the unwanted child of forbidden lovers, and defying anyone present to offer proof to the contrary.

Tordalfr's fury reached such a pitch that the cloudless sky opened up and a bolt of lightning struck his outstretched hand, coalescing into the form of a throwing spear, which he hurled at his tormentor. The javelin struck Brael in the chest, hurling him backward and leaving a blackened, smoking crater where his heart had been. Tordalfr marched furiously from the village and never returned.

"The weapon known as True Name is inseparable from the history of the Seven Cities. Whenever two devils entered into a deal with one another, the offeree of the contract would seal their true name into its ornamentations, then the blade would remain in the possession of the offerer. Should the offeree fail to uphold their end of the contract, the offerer would magically learn the name from the blade, thus gaining power over they who betrayed the sacred pact.

Is there, thus, any blade with more potential? It is written that if an infernal soul could discover the true name of the weapon itself, they could draw from it every name sworn to it since the blade's creation. Imagine the power that individual would have over the Seven Cities. Imagine the proud devils who could do naught but fall to their knees.
I have sought the blade's name for centuries. With luck, when I find it, its bearer will not know the power they wield, and it will be mine."

entries.name: An Ancient True Name
entries: Since the illrigger has many viable playstyles, {@i True Name}'s shape and rarity are flexible, allowing the GM to bestow a weapon that best fits the illrigger in their party. We suggest tying this weapon into a greater story, such as a power squabble in the Seven Cities, a feud between two fiends, or even a devil trying to learn your illrigger's true name—in Hell, a devil's true name can be spoken aloud to aid in summoning the fiend or to strip them of their power (see {@book Flee, Mortals!|FleeMortals} for these mechanics). Similar rules could apply to your infernal illrigger, if you wish.

Once a character claims {@i True Name}, they might quest to find its original name, thus learning the true names of many fiends in the hells and gaining great leverage. However, the weapon's wielder will undoubtedly encounter fiends who crave the weapon for themselves—such as Infernal Chancellor Lazivos, a chancellor in the Seven Cities whose agents collect powerful relics to enable his election to the Court. You can find his stat block and more information about him in {@book Flee, Mortals!|FleeMortals}!

entries.name: The Four Sacred Artifacts
entries: Four Sacred Artifacts appeared at the dawn of the Bürach Empire, each a divine gift from the four gods: Aurelia, Galt, Maligant, and Ulmyr. These relics were given to Bürach's first emperor, Indorius I, and inherited by each of his successors.

Maligant provided the mighty sword, Dämglesvir, to slay Bürach's enemies. Galt placed a crown on Indorius I's head to signify his divine right. Ulmyr gifted the emperor an orb of foresight to make him a wise ruler. Aurelia clad him in a breastplate, wishing only to protect him and his heirs.

Many centuries later, after Emperor Leopold I was assassinated, custody of the artifacts sparked a civil war. Each of the holy treasures disappeared amid the fighting. One religiously fervent tale claims they blazed with radiant light before banishing themselves beyond mortal reach. Other rumors suggest they were each stolen or lost in various separate conspiracies. It's certain that whoever holds the Sacred Artifacts controls the fate of the Bürach Empire.

entries.name: Wielding An Artifact
entries: Before disappearing, the artifacts were tarnished and corrupted by Emperor Leopold I's delusions, cruelty, and malice. Darkness had seeped into them, transforming their divine power and purpose. Though it's heretical to suggest, some believe the artifacts' befoulment is somehow linked to the death of the gods and the growing influence of the Great Beast.

Wielding even one Sacred Artifact is difficult. Their true power can only be unlocked by practicing their use. Yet this necessitates more time exposed to the darkness that now infuses them, which can infest the wielder's body and mind.

entries.name: Attunement and Proficiency
entries: Each Sacred Artifact has three tiers of {@variantrule Attunement|XPHB} available to its user. When a character attunes to the item, they have access only to the benefits (and the curse) listed under the Aspirant tier. The Adept and Master tiers of {@variantrule {@variantrule Attunement|XPHB}|XPHB} are unlocked over time (see Attunement Milestones, below).
{@variantrule Attunement|XPHB} to a Sacred Artifact can't be voluntarily ended. If the {@variantrule Attunement|XPHB} does end, the character can attune to the item again at the Aspirant tier.

Each artifact also curses its wielder. In addition to the curse effects listed for each tier, a character attuned to a Sacred Artifact is unwilling to part with the item, keeping it within reach at all times. If the artifact's curse is ended or suppressed, the character's {@variantrule Attunement|XPHB} with that item is broken.

entries.name: Attunement Milestones
entries: To ascend to a higher tier of {@variantrule Attunement|XPHB} and unlock additional powers of a Sacred Artifact, the attuned character must achieve a specific milestone. There is no minimum level required to achieve a milestone. However, Adept-tier artifacts are appropriate for characters of level 5 to 10, while Master-tier artifacts are appropriate for characters of level 11 and above.
The GM and players should work together to create appropriate milestones for the campaign, using these examples (themed to the four artifacts) as guidance:

items: Wield {@i {@item Dämglesvir|GrimHollowCG24}} to slay a mighty foe.
Take no damage during a difficult combat.
Earn the fealty of an important ruler.
You alter a future witnessed in {@i {@item Ulmyr's Eye|GrimHollowCG24}}.

entries.name: Shared Delusions
entries: The darkness that seeped into the Sacred Artifacts causes their wielders to experience the same paranoid delusions that plagued Emperor Leopold I.

All characters attuned to a Sacred Artifact suffer the same delusions, which could include the sense of being watched, believing a {@variantrule Friendly [Attitude]|XPHB|Friendly} NPC to be {@variantrule Hostile [Attitude]|XPHB|Hostile} , or mistaking an innocent person or household pet for a monster. Characters can even experience multiple simultaneous delusions.

A character suffering a delusion can use the {@action Search|XPHB} action to discern the truth, typically by succeeding on a {@dc 20} (or higher) Wisdom ({@skill Insight|XPHB} or {@skill Perception|XPHB}) check.

If the GM is using the {@variantrule Influence Dice|GrimHollowCG24|Influence Dice rules} rules, the frequency and intensity of delusions increases while the number of dice in the Beast Pool exceeds the number of dice in the Resolve Pool.

entries.name: Blessed Wisdom
entries: Religious texts claim Ulmyr plucked one of their own eyes as a gift for the first emperor. With it, Emperor Indorius I and his descendants would act with a measure of Ulmyr's foresight and wisdom.

The eye was kept inside the Sovereign's Orb, a golden reliquary inlaid with jewels mined from each of Bürach's provinces. These would remind the emperor of their duty to each of the realms they ruled.
